newsitem.title: CHINA: China unlikely to cut rates soon - economist.
newsitem.headline: China unlikely to cut rates soon - economist.

text.p: China is unlikely to cut interest rates in the near future to avoid a further outflow of funds from the banking system and a new speculative wave on the stock market, a senior economist said on Thursday.

Two cuts in interest rates last year had already cut dramatically into the growth rate of bank deposits and had sharply increased turnover on the nation's two stock markets. said Hu Zhuangjun, institute director of the State Council's (cabinet) Development Research Centre.
"Frankly speaking, I do not believe there will be another cut in interest rates in the near future," said the official of the top economic think tank.
"I personally believe that the stock market has risen too quickly," he told an economic forum.
"And the government, if it shares my view, will be very conservative with interest rate cuts."
China cut interest rates last year -- in May and then again in August -- as its once worrisome inflation eased.

The annual rate for one-year fixed bank deposits is now 7.47 percent, down from 9.15 percent in May 1996. Average bank deposit interest rates fell 2.48 percentage points as a result of the two cuts last year.
Retail price inflation fell to 6.1 percent last year from a communist-era high of 21.8 percent in 1994.
Inflation has continued to fall this year, with retail price inflation expected to be 3.0 to 4.0 percent -- well below the official target of 6.0 percent.
Many economists have argued that the continued decline in inflation made a further interest rate reduction possible.
Hu said last year's twin cuts had drained some 350 billion yuan ($42.17 billion) from the banking system, helping to pump up the stock market in the second half of last year and early this year.

Stock market regulators have already moved to curb the speculative stock activity with a series of measures, including an increase in the stock transaction stamp tax and brakes on stock investments by banks and state enterprises.
The economist said government policy makers also were probably concerned about the impact of an interest rate cut on efforts to market state treasury bonds.
Lower bank rates -- and lower coupon rates on state bonds -- would make it harder to attract investors to the bond market.
Hu said he did not expect the central bank to move ahead quickly with a reduction in the bank reserve ratio -- as some economists advocate -- for fear this would unleash too much cash.
